scenarios.c: Harbor Light Energy, a regional electricity and natural gas provider with 400,000 household customers
s: Last month Harbor Light Energy moved to a new billing system. Since then the call center has logged a spike in complaints: bills arriving late, estimated readings that look too high, and customers who were told two different things by two different agents.

The customer care manager (judge) is interviewing you for a customer care associate position. She wants to hear how you would handle an upset customer who calls about a bill that is nearly twice what they expected, and how you would explain company policy without sounding like you are making excuses.
n: Listens first and acknowledges the frustration before explaining anything
States the policy plainly (estimated reads, dispute window, payment plan) and why it exists
Offers a concrete next step and a follow-up date instead of a vague promise
Shows that every call represents the whole company, not just one agent
q: A customer says they will cancel service unless the late fee is removed today, but you are not allowed to waive it. What do you say?
How would you handle it if you gave a customer an answer and later found out it was wrong?

scenarios.c: Brightwave Studio, a 25-person video production company that hires freelance editors and designers
s: Brightwave Studio has always paid freelancers on a handshake. Last quarter a freelance editor delivered a project three weeks late, then claimed the studio had agreed to pay a rush bonus nobody wrote down. The studio also found out that a designer reused a client's logo artwork in her own portfolio.

The owner (judge) wants you to explain, in plain language, why written agreements matter and what the studio should put in them. She also wants to know how the studio should think about who owns creative work and what makes a promise legally binding.
p: Describe the nature of legally binding contracts
Describe methods used to protect intellectual property
Explain the nature of agency relationships
n: Names offer, acceptance and consideration as what makes an agreement binding
Explains that written terms reduce disputes about scope, price, deadlines and bonuses
Distinguishes work-for-hire from licensing and says ownership should be stated up front
Recommends having a lawyer review a standard contract template once, then reusing it
q: Is a verbal agreement ever legally binding? Why would the studio still avoid relying on one?
A freelancer is not an employee. Why does that distinction matter to the studio?

scenarios.c: Kestrel Logistics, a warehouse and delivery company that hired 60 seasonal workers in November
s: Kestrel Logistics hires dozens of seasonal workers every holiday season. Many leave within two weeks, and supervisors say new hires do not know where to go, whom to ask, or what is expected of them on day one.

The human resources director (judge) has asked you to explain what a strong orientation program includes and why it matters. She also wants to know how the company can use technology to make hiring and onboarding faster without losing the human touch.
p: Discuss the nature of human resources management
Describe the use of technology in human resources management
Explain the role of ethics in human resources management
n: Explains HRM as recruiting, training, supporting and retaining people
Covers day-one basics: safety, policies, role, supervisor, buddy, schedule
Suggests online forms, e-learning modules and a mobile schedule app
Raises fair treatment, privacy of employee data and honest job descriptions
q: A new hire tells you the job is not what they were promised in the interview. What do you do?
What information about employees should a company keep confidential, and who should see it?

scenarios.c: Greenfield Market, a four-store neighborhood grocery chain
s: Two weeks ago a customer slipped on a wet floor near the produce misters at Greenfield Market. The store had no incident report form, nobody was sure who should be told, and the same spill happened again two days later.

The operations manager (judge) wants to know how you would create a safe work environment, what the store should do the moment an accident happens, and how routine security and safety procedures help protect both employees and customers.
p: Describe health and safety regulations in business
n: Treats safety as everyone's job and names routine checks (spill logs, mats, signs)
Describes immediate steps: help the person, secure the area, report, document, follow up
Mentions workplace safety rules and why records protect the company
Links procedures to fewer injuries, lower cost and customer trust
q: An employee tells you a coworker is skipping safety steps to work faster. What do you do?
How would you decide which safety problem to fix first if you had budget for only one?

scenarios.c: Summit Health Partners, a network of eight outpatient clinics
s: Summit Health Partners is about to change its patient scheduling system. Staff are hearing about it through rumors, and front-desk employees say they do not know how to answer patients' questions.

The director of communications (judge) wants you to explain how to choose the right way to communicate the change to staff, and what makes workplace messages clear and effective. She also wants you to describe what a good staff meeting about the change would look like.
p: Explain the nature of staff communication
Choose and use appropriate channel for workplace communication
Explain the nature of effective written communications
n: Matches the message to the channel: email for details, meeting for questions, posted quick guide
Keeps messages short, specific, dated and with a named contact
Describes a meeting with an agenda, time for questions and written follow-up notes
Plans to check understanding with a short survey or manager feedback
q: Some employees say they never read company email. How would you make sure they still get the message?
How would you respond if a staff member publicly disagreed with the change during the meeting?

scenarios.c: Clearwater Medical Supply, a distributor with 220 employees
s: Clearwater Medical Supply has a 35% turnover rate in its warehouse. Exit interviews mention unclear job expectations, inconsistent supervisors and few opportunities to move up.
The human resources director (judge) wants you to explain how HR can improve retention, how to hire the right people, and how technology can support HR work.
p: Discuss the nature of human resources management
Describe the use of technology in human resources management
Explain the role of ethics in human resources management
Recognize/Reward others for their efforts and contributions
n: HR covers recruiting, hiring, training, compensation, relations and compliance
HRIS, applicant tracking and online training save time
Fair hiring, privacy, equal opportunity and honest communication
Clear job descriptions and onboarding reduce early turnover
Recognition and growth plans improve retention
q: Which would you fix first: onboarding, supervision or advancement? Why?
How would you keep an employee file confidential while still allowing managers to do their jobs?

scenarios.c: Evergreen Property Management
s: An Evergreen Property Management employee says a supervisor made repeated inappropriate comments about her. A different employee says he was passed over for promotion because of his age. The company has no formal complaint procedure.
The HR manager (judge) wants you to explain the legal issues involved, how the company should handle complaints, and what policies to put in place.
p: Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
n: Explains discrimination and harassment laws and employer responsibility
Takes complaints seriously, investigates promptly and protects against retaliation
Creates a written policy, training and a way to report
Limits information to those who need to know
Documents the process and outcome
q: An employee asks you to keep a complaint a secret. What do you say?
What could happen if the company ignores the complaints?

scenarios.c: Zenith Insurance Group
s: Zenith Insurance Group wants to create a mentoring and development program for new employees. Many new hires say they receive little feedback and do not know how to advance.
The learning and development manager (judge) wants you to explain how to plan the program, what skills it should develop and how to evaluate its success.
p: Explain the use of feedback for personal growth
Identify skills needed to enhance career progression
Explain possible advancement patterns for jobs
n: Pairs new hires with mentors and sets regular check-ins
Feedback that is specific, timely and actionable
Skills mapped to roles: communication, technology, leadership
Shows career paths with clear requirements
Measures retention, promotion rates and participant feedback
q: What would you do if mentors do not have time for mentees?
How would you convince managers to support the program?

scenarios.c: Crestline Manufacturing
s: Crestline Manufacturing recently changed work schedules from five eight-hour days to four ten-hour days. Many employees are upset and feel their concerns were ignored. Absences and complaints are rising.
The HR director (judge) wants you to explain how to communicate the change, listen to employees' concerns and rebuild trust.
p: Enlist others in working toward a shared vision
n: Explains the reasons, benefits and costs of the change honestly
Creates ways for employees to ask questions and give input
Acts on feedback where possible and explains why where not
Acknowledges emotions and listens without being defensive
Involves employee representatives in solutions
q: An employee says the change makes childcare impossible. What do you say?
How do you decide which concerns can be addressed and which cannot?

scenarios.c: Atlas Packaging
s: Atlas Packaging had three minor injuries last quarter and a workplace inspection found missing safety training records. Employees say they are rushed and sometimes skip safety steps.
The plant HR manager (judge) wants you to explain how to improve safety, what records to keep and how HR can work with supervisors.
p: Describe health and safety regulations in business
Report noncompliance with business health and safety regulations
n: Explains workplace safety requirements and employer duties
Training, equipment checks and clear signage
Describes immediate response and incident reporting
Encourages reporting without fear of retaliation
Keeps training, incident and cost records for audits
q: A supervisor tells employees to skip a safety step to meet a deadline. What do you do?
How can HR measure whether the safety program is working?

events.name: Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making

scenarios.c: Tidewater Realty, a residential real estate brokerage with 35 agents
s: Tidewater Realty's agents use personal phones and email accounts to share client documents, including mortgage pre-approvals and photo IDs. Last month an agent's phone was stolen and a client's identity information was exposed.
The managing broker (judge) has asked you and your partner to analyze the situation and recommend what the brokerage must do now and how to prevent future problems.
f: 35 agents, 600 active clients
No written policy on handling client data
Two clients have asked whether the brokerage is legally responsible
A competitor advertises 'bank-level data security'
p: Explain information privacy, security, and confidentiality considerations in business
Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
Explain the role of ethics in information management
Recognize and respond to ethical dilemmas
n: Notifies affected clients promptly and explains what happened
Names breach-notification duties and potential liability for negligence
Writes a data policy: encryption, approved storage, remote wipe, training
Explains that ethical duty goes beyond legal minimums
Offers support such as credit monitoring and a point of contact
q: Should the brokerage tell clients before it knows the full extent of the breach? Why?
What would you do if an agent refused to follow the new policy?

scenarios.c: Skyline Gym Group, a chain of fitness centers
s: Skyline Gym Group sells memberships through an online form. Many members report they could not cancel without visiting a location in person, and some say they were charged after they believed they had canceled. Two states are reviewing the gym's practices.
The chief operating officer (judge) wants you and your partner to analyze the company's exposure and recommend changes to its contracts and cancellation process.
f: 22,000 members, 18 locations
Cancellation requires in-person visit with signed form
Monthly refunds for disputed charges average $18,000
State consumer protection offices opened inquiries
p: Describe the nature of legally binding contracts
Explain legal and ethical considerations in selling
Explain the role of ethics in customer relationship management
n: Explains that contract terms must be clear, fair and not deceptive
Identifies consumer protection laws and regulatory risk
Recommends easy online cancellation, clear fees and written confirmation
Describes a complaint process and refunds for wrongful charges
Weighs short-term revenue against long-term trust
q: How much revenue might the gym lose if it makes cancellation easy, and why is it worth it?
What would you say to a member who says they were misled?

scenarios.c: Parker & Quinn Design, a small design studio owned by two friends
s: Parker & Quinn Design has grown from two friends to eight employees. The founders disagree about who makes decisions, profit is split informally, and one founder wants to leave and take a major client.
The owner (judge) wants you and your partner to analyze the business structure and recommend how to protect the company and the clients.
f: Operating as a general partnership with no written agreement
Annual revenue $640,000
One client is 30% of revenue
Founder A wants to start a competing studio
p: Explain the nature of agency relationships
Describe the nature of legally binding contracts
Describe methods used to protect intellectual property
Take responsibility for decisions and actions
n: Compares partnership with LLC and corporation: liability, taxes, control
Explains that each partner can bind the firm and be personally liable
Recommends a partnership or operating agreement, non-compete and buy-sell terms
Clarifies who owns designs and client relationships
Recommends a plan to retain the client and communicate transparently
q: How would you value the studio if one founder left?
Would you recommend an LLC? Why or why not?

scenarios.c: Beacon Learning, an online tutoring company
s: Beacon Learning allows tutors to record sessions and keeps them for quality review. A parent has asked for all recordings of her 14-year-old to be deleted. The company's policy is unclear and tutors sometimes share clips on social media for marketing.
The chief executive officer (judge) wants you and your partner to recommend how the company should manage recordings and student information.
f: 8,000 student accounts, 400 tutors
Recordings stored indefinitely
Marketing team used five student clips last month
No policy on parental consent
p: Explain legal issues associated with information management
Explain the role of ethics in information management
Explain ethical considerations in providing information
n: Recognizes extra protections for minors' information
Gets clear consent before recording or sharing clips
Sets retention limits and deletion on request
Restricts access and trains tutors and marketers
Balances business needs with student privacy
q: Should the company continue to use student clips in marketing if parents consent? Why?
What would you do if a tutor shared a clip without permission?

scenarios.c: Redline Motors, a car dealership group
s: A Redline Motors salesperson sold a used car without telling the buyer it had been in a flood. A mechanic reported it to the manager, who told him to stay quiet because the car was sold 'as is'. The mechanic is now being treated coldly by coworkers.
The general manager (judge) wants you and your partner to analyze the situation and recommend what the dealership should do now and what it should do to build an ethical culture.
f: The car was sold for $14,200
The dealership sells 900 cars a year
The mechanic has worked there for six years
An online review mentioned 'questionable practices' last month
p: Recognize and respond to ethical dilemmas
Explain the nature of organizational culture
n: Defines ethics as principles of right and wrong that guide behavior
Explains pressure to hit sales numbers as a cause of ethical lapses
Contacts the buyer, discloses and offers a remedy
Protects the mechanic from retaliation
Sets clear standards, training and a safe way to report concerns
q: The 'as is' clause may be legal. Why does that not end the discussion?
What would you do if the salesperson who sold the car is the top performer?

scenarios.c: Pedal & Pour, a planned mobile coffee bike cart for downtown offices
scenarios.j: small business advisor at a community bank
s: You want to open a bicycle-powered coffee cart that serves office workers and commuters downtown. You have savings, a few friends willing to help part time, and a lot of enthusiasm, but you have never run a business.

The advisor (judge) at your community bank offers free sessions to new entrepreneurs. She wants you to explain what entrepreneurship is, what an owner actually has to do besides making coffee, and why starting small can still matter to a local economy.
scenarios.m: the advisor's office at the bank
p: Explain the role requirements of entrepreneurs and owners
Identify the impact of small business/entrepreneurship on market economies
n: Defines entrepreneurship as taking risk to create and run a business that meets a need
Lists owner duties: finance, permits, suppliers, marketing, hiring, customer service, record keeping
Explains jobs, competition and local spending created by small firms
Compares sole proprietorship, partnership and LLC in terms of control and liability
q: What is the biggest risk in your plan, and how would you reduce it?
If a friend wanted to be your partner, what would you want in writing first?

scenarios.c: Trailhead Outfitters, a start-up that rents camping gear online
scenarios.j: attorney who volunteers at a small business clinic
s: Trailhead Outfitters lets customers rent tents, stoves and backpacks for weekend trips. Last month a customer returned a damaged tent and refused to pay, saying nobody told him about a damage fee. Another customer was injured when a camp stove failed.
The attorney (judge) wants you to explain the basic legal issues a new business owner faces and how Trailhead can protect itself with sound agreements, insurance and compliance with the law.
p: Describe the nature of legally binding contracts
Identify the basic torts relating to business enterprises
Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
n: Explains that clear rental terms, fees and signatures create enforceable agreements
Names negligence and product liability as risks when equipment fails
Recommends liability insurance, equipment inspection and maintenance logs
Stresses following the intent of laws, not only the minimum, to protect customers and reputation
q: Is a sign saying 'rent at your own risk' enough to protect the company? Why or why not?
What licenses or permits would you check on before opening?

scenarios.c: Loop Threads, a small clothing label that turns recycled fabric into jackets
s: Loop Threads sold 300 jackets last year at an average price of $85. The founder wants a $20,000 loan to buy a second sewing machine and more fabric, but the loan officer says the application is missing basic financial information.
The loan officer (judge) wants you to explain what financial statements a new business should keep, what each one tells a lender, and how you would show that the business can repay the loan.
p: Describe the need for financial information
Describe the nature of income statements
Explain the nature of balance sheets
Describe the nature of cash flow statements
n: Says financial records show how the business is doing and support decisions and loans
Income statement: revenue minus costs equals profit over a period
Balance sheet: assets, liabilities and owner's equity at one date
Cash flow statement: money in and out, showing whether payments can be made on time
q: Your business is profitable on paper but you are short on cash each month. How can that happen?
What would you do if sales dropped 20% after you received the loan?

scenarios.c: Fresh Route, a start-up delivering weekly boxes of locally grown vegetables
scenarios.j: mentor from the local chamber of commerce
s: Fresh Route has 40 subscribers after three months. Growth has stalled, and the founders are not sure whether customers want lower prices, more variety, or something else entirely.
The mentor (judge) wants you to explain how marketing helps a small business grow, what influences why customers buy, and what marketing activities Fresh Route should focus on first.
scenarios.m: the chamber of commerce conference room
p: Explain marketing and its importance in a global economy
Describe marketing functions and related activities
Explain factors that influence customer/client/business buying behavior
Determine ways of reinforcing the company's image through employee performance
n: Defines marketing as creating, communicating and delivering value to customers
Lists product, price, place, promotion plus research and selling
Cites needs, price, convenience, trust, reviews and habits as buying influences
Explains that every driver and packer reinforces the brand promise
q: How would you find out why customers cancel before spending money on ads?
Which one marketing activity would you start this month, and what result would you look for?

scenarios.c: Spark Repair, a two-person phone and laptop repair shop in a college town
s: Spark Repair is busiest in September and nearly empty in July. A larger chain is opening a kiosk across the street, and one of the two technicians wants to leave to start her own shop.
The business coach (judge) wants you to explain how an owner manages risk, what factors affect how a business is managed, and how you would respond to the new competitor and the possible departure.
p: Explain the nature of risk management
Conduct a risk assessment of an event
n: Management means planning, organizing, leading and controlling resources to reach goals
Names factors such as competition, seasonality, staff, technology and regulation
Describes identifying risks, judging likelihood and impact, and planning responses
Applies it to the competitor and the technician: cross-training, agreements, loyalty offers
q: Which risk would you handle first, the competitor or losing your technician? Why?
How would you plan for the slow summer months so the shop can cover rent?

scenarios.c: Kindred Candles, a hand-poured soy candle company run from a rented kitchen space
s: Kindred Candles sells at weekend markets and through a small online store. Monthly sales average $6,000, and the founder wants to take over a storefront. An investor has agreed to listen to the pitch.
The investor (judge) wants you to explain the opportunity, what the owner will do to manage risk, and how the investor would earn a return.
p: Explain the role requirements of entrepreneurs and owners
n: Explains the opportunity: demand, margins, loyal customers
Describes the owner's responsibilities beyond production
Considers new products, wholesale and seasonal packs
Names risks: rent, supply costs and seasonality, with plans to reduce them
Identifies competitors and how Kindred stands out
q: Why should I invest in your business instead of a store that is already established?
What would you do if sales did not rise after opening the storefront?

scenarios.c: PixelPress, a custom 3D printing service for hobbyists
s: PixelPress wants a $25,000 loan to buy two larger printers. Revenue last year was $90,000, but expenses are high and the owner is not sure how to set prices.
The loan officer (judge) wants you to explain how to price services, what financial records you would show, and how the printers would pay for themselves.
p: Describe the nature of income statements
Explain the nature of break-even analysis
n: Pricing includes materials, time, equipment, overhead and desired profit
Prepares a budget for the next year
Income statement shows revenue, costs and profit
Break-even shows how many jobs are needed to cover the new cost
Keeps organized records to support the request
q: What if a competitor cuts prices by 20%?
What would you do if you could not make a loan payment?

scenarios.c: Pawfect Walks, a dog walking and pet care service
s: Pawfect Walks has twelve regular clients but growth has plateaued. Most customers come from word of mouth and the owner does not have a marketing plan.
The mentor (judge) wants you to explain how to identify target customers, what makes the service different and how to reach new clients on a small budget.
p: Explain the concept of market and market identification
Explain the nature of marketing plans
Describe word-of-mouth channels used to communicate with targeted audiences
Describe referral programs that can be used to build brand/promote products
n: Targets busy professionals and apartment dwellers near a defined area
Plan includes goals, budget, message and timeline
Uses reviews, social posts and neighbor groups
Offers referral rewards
Plans each contact from first inquiry to follow-up
q: How would you handle a client who wants a discount for referring friends?
What would make you decide to hire an employee?

scenarios.c: Glow Up Salon, a new hair salon
s: Glow Up Salon has leased a space, hired three stylists and begun selling hair products. The owner has not decided on the business structure, has not obtained an insurance policy, and plans to treat the stylists as independent contractors.
The attorney (judge) wants you to explain the legal choices the owner must make and what risks come with each.
p: Explain legal and ethical considerations in selling
Explain the nature of agency relationships
Describe methods used to protect intellectual property
n: Compares sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC and corporation by liability and taxes
Notes licensing, insurance, lease obligations and contracts
Product claims must be truthful and safe
Employee versus contractor classification affects control, taxes and responsibility
Protects the brand name and logo
q: Should the stylists be employees or contractors? Why?
What happens if a customer is injured in the salon?

scenarios.c: Greenleaf Cafe, a successful cafe considering opening a second location
s: Greenleaf Cafe has earned a profit for three years and has loyal customers. The co-owners disagree about whether to open a second location now or wait.
The business advisor (judge) wants you to explain how to analyze the decision, what risks to consider and what steps to take if the cafe expands.
p: Conduct a risk assessment of an event
Explain the role of situation analysis in the marketing planning process
Explain the nature of risk management
n: Management involves planning, organizing, leading and controlling
Assesses the likelihood and impact of each risk
Situation analysis looks at strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
Develops contingency plans, such as reserves and phased openings
Uses data to make the decision and sets measures to review it
q: What would you do if the second location lost money for six months?
How would you maintain quality at both sites?

scenarios.c: Trailmix Bakery, a small bakery with online orders
s: Trailmix Bakery's sales are growing, but the owner has little cash in the bank. She must decide whether to buy a $22,000 commercial oven that would double output or keep outsourcing some baking at a higher cost.
The owner (judge) wants you and your partner to analyze the financial picture and recommend what to do.
f: Monthly revenue $28,000; monthly expenses $25,500
Cash on hand $6,000
Oven financing: $22,000 over 4 years at 9%
Outsourcing adds $2.10 per loaf; 2,000 loaves per month
Oven would increase capacity by 1,800 loaves
p: Describe the nature of cash flow statements
Explain the nature of break-even analysis
n: Calculates the monthly payment and compares to outsourcing savings
Considers whether the oven can be paid for from added profit
Uses break-even to show how many loaves are needed
Identifies risk if demand falls or the oven breaks
Mentions competitors and how extra capacity could grow sales
q: What would you do if sales stayed flat after buying the oven?
Would you recommend leasing instead of buying? Why?

scenarios.c: Glimmer Skincare, an online skincare brand
s: Glimmer Skincare has loyal online customers but wants to add a retail partner. A national drugstore chain has offered to stock the product if Glimmer lowers its price and pays for in-store displays.
The founder (judge) wants you and your partner to analyze the offer and recommend whether Glimmer should accept it.
f: Online price $32; cost to make $9
Retail partner wants to sell at $24 and buy at $14
Display cost: $18,000
Retailer would carry in 800 stores
Online sales: $2.4 million per year
p: Explain the nature of channels of distribution
Identify the elements of the promotional mix
Describe the nature of product/service branding
Explain the nature of marketing plans
n: Compares margin online and at retail
Considers brand image and effects on existing customers
Estimates volume needed to cover display costs
Describes promotions to support the launch
Suggests a pilot or negotiated terms
q: How might the retail price affect how customers see the brand?
What would you do if the retailer asked for exclusivity?

scenarios.c: Quick Fix Repair, a growing home repair service with 12 technicians
s: Quick Fix Repair is growing fast. Technicians are often late, customers complain about inconsistent quality, and the best technician has said she may leave to start her own business.
The owner (judge) wants you and your partner to recommend how to manage and keep employees while the company grows.
f: 12 technicians, 2 office staff
Customer rating: 3.9 out of 5
Technicians are paid hourly with no bonuses
Training consists of ride-alongs for one day
p: Explain the role of ethics in human resources management
Recognize/Reward others for their efforts and contributions
Explain possible advancement patterns for jobs
n: Creates a standard training program and checklist
Sets expectations for punctuality and quality
Uses incentives such as bonuses, recognition and career steps
Provides a path to lead technician or trainer
Treats employees fairly and communicates openly
q: How would you keep the top technician from leaving?
What would you do about a technician who is skilled but frequently late?

scenarios.c: Pixel Playground, a children's activity center
s: Pixel Playground is busy on weekends but empty on weekdays. A competitor opened nearby, and a school has asked about renting space for after-school care. The owner is unsure whether to serve a new market.
The owner (judge) wants you and your partner to recommend a strategy for the next year.
f: Weekend attendance: 280 children; weekday: 35
Fixed costs $18,000 per month
After-school program could bring 40 children, 5 days per week
Staffing for the program: 3 additional employees
p: Explain the role of situation analysis in the marketing planning process
Conduct a risk assessment of an event
Explain the nature of marketing plans
n: Analyzes strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
Compares revenue and cost of the after-school program
Identifies risks: safety, licensing, staffing, liability
Recommends measurable goals and a pilot period
Considers other opportunities such as birthday parties and camps
q: How would you decide if the after-school program is working?
What licensing or safety steps would you take first?

scenarios.c: Blue Door Consulting, a two-person consulting firm
s: Blue Door Consulting's two founders have different working styles. One wants to grow quickly by hiring; the other wants to stay small. They argue about priorities, and a key client has noticed.
The owner (judge) wants you and your partner to recommend how the founders can resolve their differences and align on a shared vision.
f: Revenue: $420,000; two clients account for 55%
One founder prefers hiring two employees now
Other founder fears losing quality and control
Client said, 'You two need to get on the same page'
p: Enlist others in working toward a shared vision
n: Encourages each founder to explain their goals and concerns
Finds common goals such as stability and growth
Suggests a trial hire or phased plan
Sets decision rules and regular check-ins
Considers outside help such as a mediator or advisor
q: What if the founders cannot agree after the discussion?
How would you keep disagreements from affecting clients?

scenarios.c: Cedar Ridge Credit Union, a community credit union with 22,000 members
s: Cedar Ridge Credit Union is launching a financial wellness program for first-time account holders. Many young members are using debit cards but do not understand credit, interest or budgeting.
The branch manager (judge) wants you to explain the purpose and importance of credit, how to calculate and control its cost, and what a first-time borrower should know before applying for a loan.
p: Explain the purposes and importance of credit
Demonstrate the wise use of credit
n: Credit lets people buy now and pay later, but it has a cost and builds a history
Cost of credit = interest plus fees over the life of the loan; APR helps compare
Advises paying on time, borrowing only what is needed, and keeping balances low
Walks through a loan application: income, credit history, purpose, terms, comparing offers
q: A member wants to borrow $3,000 on a credit card instead of a loan. What would you ask them first?
How does missing a payment affect a person's future borrowing?

scenarios.c: Northbridge Financial, a regional bank
s: Northbridge Financial is training new employees on the legal duties that come with handling other people's money. Last quarter an employee emailed a customer's account details to a personal address to 'finish work at home.'

The compliance officer (judge) wants you to explain why financial firms must follow laws and regulations, what the spirit and intent of those rules is, and how a banker should handle customer information.
p: Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
Explain legal responsibilities associated with financial exchanges

Explain the need for ongoing education as a worker

Explain the nature of accounts receivable

Keeps records in a consistent system with dates, amounts and approvals

How often should the practice reconcile its bank account, and why?

scenarios.c: BrightPath Learning Center, a childcare and tutoring center with 35 employees

Keeps confidential data secure

s: Spark Photo Booth has been open for six months and is booked nearly every weekend in spring. The co-owners want to buy two more booths for $11,000 each and hire a part-time attendant. They are asking a local bank for a $22,000 loan. The loan officer has questions about the business plan, the legal setup and the risks.

The loan officer (judge) wants to understand how you run the business day to day, how you will manage employees and records, what insurance and legal protections you have, and what happens if bookings fall during the off-season.
You have 7 minutes to present the business, compare the choices (buy two booths, buy one, or lease), and recommend one.

Operating costs: supplies and travel about $60 per event; insurance $55 a month
Two new booths: $22,000 total; one new booth: $11,000; leasing: $380 a month per booth
Off-season (July to September) typically has only 2 or 3 events a month
The business is an LLC with two co-owners and no employees yet
n: Explains the day-to-day activities of running the venture, including scheduling and customer service
Describes the business structure (LLC) and why liability protection matters
Compares buying two, buying one and leasing, with pros and cons including seasonality
Shows that revenue ($13,950 so far) can cover loan payments with a safety margin
Discusses insurance, contracts and employee requirements for the part-time attendant
Recommends the most prudent option and a plan for the slow season
q: How would you pay the loan during the three slow months?
What happens if a booth is damaged at a client's event?
Why do you need two booths rather than one?

scenarios.c: Harvest Box, a startup that sells weekly boxes of locally grown produce
s: Harvest Box buys vegetables from six local farms and delivers weekly boxes to 140 subscribers. The founders are about to sign a contract with a large office complex to deliver 200 boxes a week. The attorney (judge) has agreed to give you a short consultation. The attorney wants to know what you are doing now, what you plan to do, and how you would manage legal risk as the business grows.
You have 7 minutes to explain your situation, compare the legal options available to you, and recommend what to do before signing the new contract.
f: Current structure: sole proprietorship owned by one founder; the co-founder is paid as a contractor
Revenue: $9,800 a month from 140 subscribers
The office contract is for 12 months and would add about $5,400 a month
Insurance: none beyond a general home policy
Legal costs: forming an LLC is about $500; a contract review is $350; business insurance is about $900 a year
n: Identifies the risks of a sole proprietorship, including unlimited personal liability
Compares staying as is, forming an LLC and forming a corporation with pros and cons
Lists licenses, permits and food-safety requirements to check
Explains why a contract review and liability insurance matter before signing
Distinguishes an employee from an independent contractor
Recommends the order of steps and the costs, about $1,750 in total
q: What would happen to your personal savings if a customer got sick?
Should the co-founder be an owner, an employee or a contractor?
What clause in the office contract worries you the most?

s: Alder Outdoor Gear sells only in the United States. A distributor in Germany has offered to carry its backpacks in 300 stores. Canada: three retailers would order 2,500 backpacks in year one; wholesale price $58

scenarios.c: Delmar Tile Company, an importer of ceramic tile from three countries
s: The government has announced a new 20 percent tariff on ceramic tile from one of Delmar's three suppliers, the one that provides 55 percent of the company's tile. New tariff cost: about $462,000 per year on the affected supplier's tile
Delmar's net profit last year: $380,000

scenarios.c: Nova Fitness, a gym equipment company considering a new factory abroad
s: Nova Fitness is considering building a factory in one of two countries. Country X has a market economy with low taxes and strong property rights but higher wages. Country Y has a government-planned economy with heavy state involvement, lower wages, and rules that require partnering with a state-owned company. Both countries have growing middle classes.

A board member (judge) wants to understand how the economic system of each country would affect Nova's costs, risks and freedom to operate, and which country the company should choose. The board can invest up to $6 million.
You have 7 minutes to compare the economic systems, explain the alternatives and recommend where to build.
f: Country X: factory cost $5.4 million; labor $14 an hour; corporate tax 18%
Country Y: factory cost $4.1 million; labor $6 an hour; corporate tax 25%; a state partner would hold 40% of the business
Country X has well-protected property rights and independent courts
In Country Y, prices of some inputs are set by the government and approvals can take 9 to 14 months
Projected annual output: 40,000 machines in either location
n: Explains market, command and mixed economies and how each treats prices, ownership and competition
Compares costs including labor, tax and the ownership share required in Country Y
Discusses the risk of delays, price controls and unclear property rights
Includes at least three options, such as X, Y with a partner, or exporting from a third country
Recommends one with clear reasons, probably Country X or a staged entry
Names factors that would change the choice
q: Why not simply pick the cheaper labor?
What does a 40 percent state partner mean for decision making?
How would you protect Nova's designs in each country?

scenarios.c: Sunny Valley Naturals, a company that sells herbal teas and supplements
s: Sunny Valley Naturals wants to ship its products to Japan and Australia after an online retailer there offered to sell them. A friend warned that each country has its own labeling, ingredient and customs rules and that some supplement ingredients are restricted. The owner worries about being fined or having a shipment seized.

The owner (judge) wants you to explain the legal and regulatory issues in exporting, how contracts and responsibilities should be handled, and what steps the company should take before shipping. The owner is also interested in whether to start with the teas only.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis and recommendation.
f: Current products: 8 teas and 5 supplements; supplements make up 60% of U.S. sales
Japan and Australia require ingredient review and local-language labeling for supplements
Customs paperwork errors can delay shipments for weeks and may lead to fines
A trade attorney charges $2,500 to review labels and contracts for one country
Initial order from the retailer: $18,000 in teas and $30,000 in supplements
scenarios.d: present your compliance analysis and recommendation
n: Identifies key legal issues: product regulation, labeling, customs documents and contract terms
Explains who is responsible for compliance in an international sale (the exporter, importer and shipper)
Compares shipping everything, starting with teas only, or delaying until reviewed, with pros and cons
Estimates compliance costs and ties them to the size of the order
Recommends a safer first shipment and a plan for supplements
Mentions insurance, shipping terms and dispute resolution in the contract
q: Which of the two countries would you handle first, and why?
What could go wrong if a supplement ingredient is banned?
Who pays if the shipment is seized?

scenarios.c: Brightline Electronics, a company that assembles tablets in the United States for sale in several countries
s: Brightline assembles tablets in the U.S. and exports about a third of its output. Over the last six months the dollar has strengthened by 12 percent against other major currencies, and Brightline's foreign sales have dropped. The company's overseas customers now pay more in their own currencies for the same tablet.

The chief financial officer (judge) wants to know how the exchange rate change affects the company and what Brightline should do: cut prices abroad, move some assembly overseas, buy currency hedges or wait for the dollar to weaken.
You have 7 minutes to explain the economics, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend a plan.
f: Export sales dropped from $18 million to $14.5 million in six months
Average price of a tablet: $300 in the U.S.; a Euro customer's price rose from about 270 to 303 euros
Moving final assembly overseas would take 14 months and cost $4.5 million
Hedging the next year of sales would cost about 1.5% of sales ($210,000)
Price cuts of 8% abroad would reduce profit margin from 22% to about 15% on those sales
n: Explains how a stronger dollar makes exports more expensive and imports cheaper
Uses supply, demand and elasticity ideas to explain the fall in foreign sales
Compares at least three options with the cost and benefit of each
Calculates the effect of price cuts and hedging costs
Recommends a plan, such as a hedge now and a long-term review of local assembly
Names what would happen if the dollar reverses
q: How can the same tablet cost more for a customer abroad if we did not raise our price?
Is it better to protect margin or volume?
What signal would tell you to stop hedging?

scenarios.c: Skyline Appliances, a retailer of home appliances with an online store and two showrooms
s: Mr. Alvarez bought a $1,150 washing machine from Skyline Appliances three weeks ago. Delivery was supposed to take 5 days, but it arrived on day 14, and the installer left without hooking up the water line because the hose was not included. Mr. Alvarez has taken two days off work waiting for fixes and has now called the store, angry, and says he wants to cancel the order and get his money back.

You are the customer service representative who answers the call. Store policy allows you to offer a delivery fee refund ($79), a free installation kit ($35 value), a 10 percent discount on future purchases, or a full return if the item is unused. A full return of an installed machine requires manager approval and a $60 pickup fee.
The judge will play Mr. Alvarez. You have 7 minutes to understand his concerns, solve the problem and close the conversation so he is satisfied.
f: Purchase: $1,150 washing machine, paid in full
Delivery promised in 5 days; delivered on day 14
Installer did not connect the machine; the hose kit was missing
Customer has missed two days of work
Options: delivery fee refund ($79), free install kit ($35), 10% off a future purchase, or a return with a $60 pickup fee
scenarios.m: a phone call at the customer service desk

Explains policy plainly and offers the return option if he still prefers it
Shows empathy and diplomacy throughout and avoids blaming other employees
Confirms that he is satisfied and follows up to prevent a repeat
q: Do you have any idea how much time I have lost on this?
Why should I trust that the next installer will actually show up?
I think I just want my money back. Can you do that?

scenarios.c: Maple Grove Inn, a 60-room hotel that prides itself on friendly service
s: Ms. Patel is traveling for a family wedding and arrives at 10 p.m. only to discover her room is not ready. The system shows it was never cleaned after the previous guest left. She is tired, has a four-year-old with her, and asks to speak to someone about the problem. The inn has one room available, a suite that costs $60 more per night, and a standard room next door that will be ready in 30 minutes.

You may offer a complimentary breakfast, a late checkout, a drink voucher, or a room upgrade at the standard rate with manager approval. The inn wants guests to feel valued and likes to turn mistakes into positive moments of truth.
The judge will play Ms. Patel. You have 7 minutes to welcome her, solve the problem and leave her with a good impression of the hotel.
f: Reservation: 2 nights in a standard room at $139 per night
The standard room needs 30 minutes of cleaning
One suite is available at $199 per night
Guest is traveling with a four-year-old
You can give breakfast vouchers, a late checkout or the suite at the standard rate with the manager's approval
scenarios.d: help the guest and resolve the situation
n: Greets her warmly, apologizes sincerely and shows she is a priority
Anticipates unspoken needs, such as a tired child, with a comfortable waiting spot and a snack
Offers real choices: wait 30 minutes or take the suite, with the manager's approval for the standard rate
Adds a small extra, such as breakfast, to turn a bad moment into a positive one
Explains what the inn will do to prevent the problem again
Confirms she is satisfied before ending the conversation
q: I booked this weeks ago. How could you not have my room ready?
I can't make my four-year-old wait around in a lobby.
If I take the suite, am I paying extra for your mistake?

scenarios.c: ClearView Software, a company that sells scheduling software to small clinics
s: Dr. Nguyen runs a six-person dental clinic and has used ClearView's scheduling software for four years. She called because the software's billing feature is down and she cannot send invoices. In addition, her renewal is due in 30 days, and a competitor has offered her a cheaper plan. She has also complained twice in the last year that nobody responded to her emails.

Your job is to solve the immediate problem, rebuild the relationship, and convince her to stay without being pushy. The company can offer a month of free service, priority support, and a loyalty discount of up to 12 percent on renewal. The billing outage is expected to last until tomorrow afternoon.
The judge will play Dr. Nguyen. You have 7 minutes to resolve the issue and keep the relationship strong.

Billing feature is down; expected fix in about 20 hours
Two unanswered emails in the past year
Competitor offer: 20% cheaper for the first year
ClearView can offer a free month, priority support and up to 12% off renewal
scenarios.m: a phone call from the account management office
scenarios.d: resolve the client's concern and discuss renewal
n: Apologizes for the outage and the unanswered emails and takes ownership
Offers a workaround for invoices today, such as a manual template, and a timeline for the fix
Uses client history from the CRM to show she is valued
Responds to the competitor offer by highlighting value and offering a fair incentive
Keeps the renewal discussion honest rather than pushy
Sets a follow-up date and gives her a direct contact
q: Why does it take two emails and a phone call to get anyone here to respond?
Another company is cheaper. Why shouldn't I switch?
What exactly will you do differently from now on?

scenarios.c: TrailPoint Outfitters, an outdoor gear store
scenarios.j: a customer, Jordan, planning a first backpacking trip
s: Jordan walks into TrailPoint Outfitters looking for a sleeping bag for a first backpacking trip next month in the mountains, where nighttime temperatures may drop to 35 degrees. Jordan has a budget of about $150 and is unsure what to buy. Two options are in stock: a $129 synthetic bag rated to 40 degrees and a $189 down bag rated to 30 degrees that is lighter and packs smaller. Jordan has already said the price of the second bag is too high.

You must find out what Jordan needs, recommend the right product, handle objections and close the sale in a way that is honest and helpful. The store also sells a $24 compression sack and a $59 sleeping pad, which would affect warmth.
The judge will play Jordan. You have 7 minutes to ask the right questions, make a recommendation and close the sale.
f: Budget: about $150
Trip: 3 nights, mountain camping, lows near 35 degrees
Option A: synthetic bag, rated 40 degrees, $129, heavier
Option B: down bag, rated 30 degrees, $189, lighter and packable
Accessories: compression sack $24; sleeping pad $59; the store offers a 30-day return policy
scenarios.d: help the customer choose and buy
n: Builds rapport and asks needs-based questions about trip, weather, weight and budget
Explains features and benefits in terms of Jordan's trip
Recommends honestly, probably Option A plus a pad, and explains why a 40-degree bag is risky at 35 degrees without a pad
Turns the price objection into a value discussion and mentions the return policy
Asks for the sale and offers add-ons without pressure
Follows up with care tips and an invitation to return after the trip
q: The $189 one is way too much. Why is it better?
Will I really be cold in the cheaper one?
What if I buy it and find out I need something different?

scenarios.c: BrightSky Mobile, a wireless service provider
s: Alex's phone bill is $212 this month, more than double the usual $89, and Alex was never told about the charges for data overage and an international call. The judge will play Alex. You have 7 minutes to calm the situation, decide on a fair solution and help Alex feel respected.

Charges: $96 data overage and $27 for an international call
Alerts were reportedly sent by text, but Alex says none arrived
Credit allowed without approval: up to $100
Other options: payment plan, free usage alert, a plan change to $65 unlimited data

scenarios.d: help the customer with the bill

Treats Alex with dignity and does not accuse them of ignoring alerts

Offers a fair credit and further choices, such as a payment plan and a better-fit plan
Explains the next steps and checks that the solution works for Alex
Records the case in the customer record so the problem does not repeat

I can't pay $212 this month. What am I supposed to do?
How do I know this won't happen again?

You have 7 minutes to present your analysis, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and make a recommendation.

Last full backup: three weeks old
